questions.question: BrightCart's Q1 sessions grew from 200,000 (Jan) to 240,000 (Mar), but orders only grew from 8,000 to 7,920. What happened to the Session-to-Order conversion rate?
options: It rose from 3.3% to 4.0%
It fell from 4.0% to 3.3%
It stayed flat at 4.0%
It cannot be calculated from this data
questions.explanation: Jan conversion = 8,000/200,000 = 4.0%. Mar conversion = 7,920/240,000 = 3.3%. Traffic grew but conversion eroded — a classic case where a vanity metric (sessions) masks a deteriorating core metric (conversion).

questions.question: In the BrightCart Q1 capstone, Gross Revenue grew ~4% but Net Revenue was essentially flat. Using the metric tree, what is the dominant driver of the gap?
options: A drop in Average Order Value
Returns growing from 10% of gross revenue in January to 14% in March
A decline in sessions
An increase in COGS
questions.explanation: Net Revenue = Gross Revenue minus Returns. Returns grew from $64,000 (10% of $640,000 gross) to $93,139 (14% of $665,280 gross), absorbing nearly all of the gross revenue gain. Driver decomposition isolates this by holding other levers constant.

questions.question: Why must Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC) be segmented by sales channel for a company like BrightCart that sells via web and a marketplace partner?
options: CCC is only relevant to SaaS companies
Marketplace payouts often follow a fixed delayed schedule (e.g., bi-weekly) regardless of sale date, while web sales settle near-instantly via card — blending them distorts Days Sales Outstanding
CCC cannot include inventory data
Channels never affect days payable outstanding
questions.explanation: DSO depends heavily on payment timing mechanics, which differ structurally between channels. Averaging an instant-settlement channel with a delayed-payout channel produces a blended DSO that doesn't represent either channel accurately.

questions.question: BrightCart loses 4,000 of 50,000 active customers in Q1 (logo churn), but those customers represented only $180,000 of a $7,200,000 trailing revenue base. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Logo churn (8%) and revenue churn (2.5%) should be averaged into a single 5.25% churn figure
Only revenue churn (2.5%) should be reported, since it is the more favorable number
Both figures should be reported explicitly — logo churn is over 3x revenue churn, indicating the customers leaving are disproportionately low-value
Only logo churn (8%) should be reported, since it is the more conservative number
questions.explanation: Logo churn and revenue churn measure different things (customer count vs. dollar value) and can diverge significantly. Reporting both, explicitly labeled, gives leadership the full picture: a volume problem in low-value segments, not a high-value retention crisis.

questions.question: BrightCart's wholesale team signs a $120,000, 12-month supply contract in March, with even monthly delivery. How much should count as Q1 *revenue* (not bookings)?
options: The full $120,000, since the contract is signed
$0, since no cash has been collected yet
Approximately $10,000 — the portion of the contract delivered in March
$60,000, half the annual contract value
questions.explanation: Bookings reflect signed commitments; revenue is recognized as goods/services are delivered. Only the delivered portion (1/12th of the annual contract, recognized in March) counts as Q1 revenue under standard accrual recognition (e.g., ASC 606).

questions.question: A marketing ROAS calculation attributes $80,000 of revenue to a $20,000 paid social campaign using last-touch attribution. Why might this overstate the channel's true value?
options: Last-touch attribution always understates every channel

Last-touch gives 100% of credit to the final click before purchase, which often rewards a 'closing' channel like retargeting social even when an earlier channel (e.g., email or organic search) actually drove discovery
ROAS cannot be calculated with last-touch data
Paid social campaigns never have measurable ROAS
questions.explanation: Attribution model choice materially changes which channel gets credit. Multi-touch or data-driven attribution would split credit across the full path, often revealing that a 'closing' channel like paid social looks artificially strong under last-touch.

questions.question: Why is Win Rate calculated only on closed (won + lost) deals, excluding deals still open in the pipeline?
options: Open deals always count as losses
Including open deals in the denominator inflates the win rate by diluting it with pipeline that hasn't lost yet
Open deals always count as wins
Win rate cannot be calculated with open deals in the data at all
questions.explanation: Win Rate = Won / (Won + Lost). Open, in-progress deals haven't resolved either way; including them in the denominator artificially lowers the apparent loss rate and inflates the win rate, masking the team's true closing performance.

questions.question: BrightCart's warehouse On-Time Delivery Rate drops from 95% to 88% during peak season. Two weeks later, support tickets spike. What does this connection illustrate about metric trees?
options: Operations metrics and customer-facing metrics are unrelated

An operational lever (delivery SLA) feeds into a downstream outcome (support volume), so root-causing a customer experience problem may require tracing back to an operations metric, not just the customer-facing one
Support ticket volume always causes delivery delays
On-time delivery rate has no business impact
questions.explanation: Metric trees connect operational levers (like fill rate or on-time delivery) to downstream financial and experience outcomes. A spike in support tickets is often a lagging indicator of an operational root cause that occurred earlier in the chain.
